headline: No arXiv listing has gone out since Friday, so the weekend's sharpest result is Friday's: a single lithium tantalate chip that makes, modulates and reads signals from 100 GHz to 2.5 THz with optical fibre as its only link to the outside.

items.title: A terahertz front end whose only connections are optical fibres
items.dek: Jiawen Liu, Ileana-Cristina Benea-Chelmus and nine co-authors built one lithium tantalate photonic chip that generates, modulates, routes and detects continuous-wave signals from 100 GHz to 2.5 THz, reaching it only through optical fibre.
items.why_it_matters: Above roughly 100 GHz the lossiest part of a measurement chain is usually the cable and the probe, and inside a cryostat those same cables are the dominant heat leak. Putting generation and detection on one die removes both problems at once: the signal never leaves the chip as an electrical wave, and what crosses the temperature boundary is a fibre carrying milliwatts of light rather than metal carrying heat.
items.background_md: Between about 100 GHz and a few terahertz neither electronics nor optics is comfortable. Transistor amplifiers run out of gain, and coaxial cable and metal waveguide attenuate steeply because conductor loss grows roughly as the square root of frequency while the usable cross-section shrinks. Electro-optics is one way around that gap: in a material whose refractive index shifts linearly with applied field — the Pockels effect — an optical carrier and a terahertz field can exchange energy, so a terahertz tone can be synthesised as the beat note between two optical tones and read back by the reverse process.
items.deeper_md:
The platform is 600 nm of x-cut lithium tantalate on 4.7 µm of buried oxide, with rib waveguides etched 350 nm deep and gold coplanar striplines at a nominal 200 nm gap. Two racetrack resonators, loaded Q about 1.2×10⁶ and free spectral range near 36 GHz, sit 12 µm apart and are coupled only through that stripline. Pumping different pairs of optical modes steps the terahertz frequency in whole multiples of the FSR, and at 5, 10 and 15 FSRs — 180, 360 and 540 GHz — generator and detector are resonant at once, making the response about 10 dB stronger than at neighbouring frequencies. Peak drive-normalised conversion is 1.0%/mW generating at 720 GHz and 0.5%/mW detecting at 864 GHz, with g₀/2π near 10 kHz from 180 to 900 GHz. At 4 K on a dilution refrigerator's still plate it produced sidebands from 178 to 576 GHz on 2.6 mW of pump.

Two limits the authors state: the strong frequencies are pinned to integer multiples of a fixed 36 GHz FSR, so this is not a tunable source; and stripline attenuation climbs with frequency, with a power-law exponent of 0.73 below 700 GHz and 1.69 above, which removes the resonant enhancement past roughly 1.5 THz.

glossary.definition: A linear change in a material's refractive index with applied electric field, present only in crystals without inversion symmetry; it is what lets an optical and a terahertz field trade energy in the same waveguide.
The frequency spacing between adjacent resonances of a ring or racetrack cavity, set by its round-trip length; here about 36 GHz, which quantises every terahertz frequency the chip can enhance.

The single-photon electro-optic coupling rate — how strongly one terahertz photon shifts one optical photon's frequency — and the figure of merit that says whether a device works at quantum-level drive rather than only at high power.

A resonator's stored energy divided by the energy lost per cycle including the loss to the waveguide that feeds it; 1.2×10⁶ here means light circulates roughly a million cycles, which is where the field build-up comes from.

items.fab_angle: The electrode gap is 200 nm filled with 300 nm of gold laid down by lift-off rather than etched, so the aspect ratio across the gap is greater than one. Lift-off puts the whole resolution burden on the resist profile, because the metal has to break at an undercut instead of being patterned after deposition — which is why the resist sidewall, not the exposure dose, is the parameter that decides whether a gap that narrow survives.

sources.title: All-photonic millimeter-wave and terahertz signal core at room and cryogenic temperatures

items.title: Piston micromirrors beat tilting ones at twice the beam radius
items.dek: Jaekwon Lee, David Miller, Olav Solgaard and two co-authors steered nine optical channels with a Texas Instruments phase-only micromirror array — mirrors that move up and down instead of tilting — and held worst-case crosstalk to −21.7 dB at a channel spacing of twice the beam radius.
items.why_it_matters: An ideal flat tilting mirror cannot get to −20 dB at that spacing; the theoretical figure is −16.2 dB, because a tilted flat facet throws a diffraction pattern whose sidelobes land on the neighbouring receivers. A piston array synthesises an arbitrary phase profile instead, so the sidelobes can be steered into the gaps, and channel density stops being set by the mechanical angle a mirror can reach.
items.background_md: A free-space optical interconnect carries each channel as a beam across open space between two arrays of steerable mirrors rather than down a fibre or a waveguide. Its attraction is that channel count grows with area in two dimensions, while a waveguide bus grows in one. What limits it is crosstalk: a beam aimed at one receiver always deposits some power on the receivers beside it, and how much depends on the diffraction pattern the steering element imposes. Above that sits a hard ceiling — the number of orthogonal wave channels two apertures of a given size and separation support at all.
items.deeper_md:
The modulator is a TI phase light modulator: 1358×800 micromirrors on a 10.8 µm pitch, 94.5% fill factor, four bits of height per mirror, driven at 450 nm and mounted near 45° so the effective stroke falls by √2. Nine 3×3 reflectors of 98×62 pixels each were optimised by gradient ascent, with the gradient estimated from Hadamard-pattern perturbations in stages from 3×3 to 36×36 per channel, against an objective of each channel's signal minus its strongest neighbour's leakage. Loading the analytic tip-tilt phase onto the piston array gives −4.7 dB; optimising gives −21.7 dB at a pitch of two beam radii, at an average signal cost of 1.24 dB. At 2.33 and 3.09 beam radii the measurement hits the camera noise floor at about −24 dB.

The caveats are large. Nine channels were built; 156 on one chip and 10,000 across three reticles are projections, and reaching −20 dB at 10,000 channels needs a piston pitch of 360 nm or less. Switching ran under 1 Hz, limited by the mirrors and the camera, and the authors flag yield as the open question for piston mirrors at scale.

glossary.definition: A mirror that translates along its surface normal, changing the optical path length rather than the reflection angle; an array of them writes a phase map, which is what makes an arbitrary beam shape possible.
The power a channel leaks into its most strongly coupled neighbour, in decibels relative to its own signal; the worst neighbour, not the average, is what sets the link's error rate.
The fraction of an array's area that is active mirror rather than gap; the gaps scatter light into unwanted orders, so 94.5% here is a direct limit on how much power reaches the intended channel.

Sixteen available mirror heights, so any phase profile is quantised to sixteen levels; the quantisation error scatters power out of the designed pattern, which is where most of the 1.24 dB signal loss comes from.

items.fab_angle: A DMD tilts and a phase light modulator pistons, and for a maskless stepper that difference is the whole argument: tilting gives you a binary on-or-off pixel, pistoning gives you a phase pixel and therefore interference between pixels. The number to watch is the ladder of sixteen heights, which is not evenly spaced — a separate characterisation of the same part found twelve of the sixteen levels crammed into the first π, so any such tool needs a per-device calibrated lookup table before a dose map means anything.

sources.title: Reconfigurable Free-Space Optical Interconnects

items.title: Nitrogen vacancies, not scandium, decide where an AlN domain starts
items.dek: Zijian Zhou, Kan-Hao Xue and ten co-authors combined density-functional theory, machine-learned molecular dynamics and sputtered Mo/AlScN/Mo capacitors to argue that missing nitrogen atoms are where polarisation reversal nucleates in aluminium nitride, and that scandium's main contribution is making more of them.
items.why_it_matters: In a vacancy-free lattice the flip is cooperative — a whole layer has to reverse together along the polar axis, and a sideways domain wall is unstable — which is why the simulated coercive field comes out above 30 MV/cm. A vacancy locally softens the stiffness along that axis and gives the reversal somewhere to begin, so the switching voltage becomes a property of the defect population rather than of the ideal crystal, and the defect population is set by the deposition recipe.
items.background_md: A ferroelectric stores a bit as the direction its internal polarisation points, not as charge on a capacitor that leaks away. Wurtzite aluminium nitride is the unusual candidate: it is already sputtered in CMOS lines, it stays polar above 600 °C, and it adds no element the back end does not already see. Its obstacle is the coercive field — the field needed to reverse the polarisation — which sits in the megavolts-per-centimetre range. That puts switching at several volts for a film thin enough to be useful, and the film cannot simply be thinned further without leaking.
items.deeper_md:
The molecular dynamics runs a learned interatomic potential on about 40,000 atoms in a 10.8 × 7.8 × 5.2 nm block. Pristine AlN switches at 30.84 MV/cm; adding roughly 1% randomly placed nitrogen vacancies drops that to 21.75 MV/cm, a 30.1% reduction. Climbing-image nudged elastic band puts the per-unit-cell switching barrier at about 1.08 eV in pristine AlN and 0.77 eV beside a vacancy; in Sc-doped AlN a vacancy on the N2 site takes 0.31 eV off, about 45%. Clustering matters because it is favourable: clustered vacancies in a 142-atom cell sit 1.17 eV lower than dispersed ones. The mechanism is elastic — a vacancy softens C₃₃ far more than C₁₁ or C₂₂, flattening the potential along exactly the axis the reversal has to travel.

The gap to shipped devices is the thing to hold onto. Simulated nucleation fields of 21–27 MV/cm are four to eight times the 3–5 MV/cm measured on real AlScN capacitors, and the authors say directly that their simulation window is too short to see late switching. The interfacial vacancy layer is prescribed, not measured, and the vacancy count in the x = 0.18 films is inferred from a weaker Al-L₂,₃ EELS doublet rather than quantified.

glossary.definition: A lattice site where a nitrogen atom is missing; the surrounding bonds relax, which both lowers the local energy cost of flipping the polarisation and makes the site a trap for leakage current.

The applied field at which a ferroelectric's polarisation reverses; multiplied by film thickness it is the switching voltage, so it is the number that decides whether a memory runs off a logic supply.
The elastic stiffness along the crystal's c axis, which in wurtzite AlN is the polar axis; softening it is what lets one unit cell invert without dragging its neighbours along.
The highest energy along the lowest-energy path between two atomic configurations, computed by relaxing a chain of intermediate images; it sets how improbable a thermally assisted flip is.

items.fab_angle: This makes nitrogen partial pressure and substrate bias during sputtering the knobs that set switching voltage, which is a tool setting rather than a materials choice. It is also why the 250 °C HiPIMS route matters: that is below the roughly 400 °C ceiling the copper wiring stack imposes, so a ferroelectric deposited that cool can be built above finished transistors instead of beside them.

sources.title: Nitrogen vacancy cluster-mediated ferroelectric domain growth in wurtzite AlN

items.title: Sweep the timing threshold and a DRAM's bank mapping becomes checkable
items.dek: Hewen Zhang and Ian Harris timed about ten million random address pairs on a Jetson Orin Nano's LPDDR5 memory and, instead of reporting one bank-address mapping, reported one mapping per timing threshold together with a test that says which of them is right.
items.why_it_matters: Which DRAM bank a physical address lands in is an exclusive-OR of selected address bits that no datasheet publishes, and every method for recovering it rests on a latency cut-off a human picked off a histogram by eye. Making that cut-off a swept parameter turns the answer into a measurement with a pass rate attached, which is the difference between a result and a result somebody else can reproduce on a part they have never seen.
items.background_md: A DRAM chip is divided into banks, each with a single row buffer. Reading a row loads it into that buffer; reading a different row in the same bank forces a write-back and a refill, which costs tens of nanoseconds more than a hit. Which bank an address reaches is decided by the memory controller, almost always as exclusive-ORs of chosen address bits, so that sequential accesses spread across banks instead of colliding. Vendors do not document those functions, so anyone who needs them — for a Rowhammer study, a side-channel analysis, a bank-aware allocator — measures them from outside by timing pairs of addresses.
items.deeper_md:
On the Jetson Orin Nano, about ten million latency samples put the boundary between same-bank and different-bank pairs somewhere in the 500–570 CPU-cycle band. Sweeping the threshold across that band and solving for candidate masks at each step — a linear-constraint solve reduced to a basis over GF(2) — produced five distinct mask sets; one of them, with seven masks, held a group-verification pass rate near 1.0 across a wide range and 0.996907 at a chosen threshold of 550 cycles, averaged over ten rounds. The second test is the elegant one. Remove one correct mask and the pass rate should fall to 0.498454, because dropping one independent XOR constraint roughly doubles the number of pairs the remaining set calls same-bank while only half of them really are. Removing each mask in turn landed near that figure. A Raspberry Pi 4B with LPDDR4 gave two candidate sets and four masks.

The limits: pass rates collapse outside the separation band, so the sweep is only as good as the histogram under it; the 0.498454 expectation assumes the two sampled events are independent; and only two ARM boards were tested, with the single-mask test run on just one of them. Runtime is not reported.

glossary.definition: Two accesses hitting the same bank but different rows, so the open row must be written back before the next is read; the extra tens of nanoseconds is the signal every one of these methods measures.
The set of physical-address bits whose exclusive-OR produces one bit of the bank index; a complete mapping is a basis of such masks, which is why recovering it is linear algebra rather than search.
Arithmetic on the two elements 0 and 1 where addition is exclusive-OR; address-scrambling functions are linear over it, so Gaussian elimination recovers an independent basis of masks.

An LPDDR5 addressing mode that splits banks into groups with their own timing constraints; because a part can run in BG, 8-bank or 16-bank mode, the part number alone does not tell you how many banks to solve for.

items.title: Updating a prefetch table with a coin flip instead of a copy
items.dek: Yinting Huang, Jacky Wong and Sam Ainsworth changed how a spatial-pattern prefetcher — hardware that guesses which cache lines a program will touch next — records what it sees: newly observed bits enter its table with probability p and absent bits leave with probability q, rather than the old pattern being overwritten.
items.why_it_matters: Overwriting the stored pattern on every observation makes the predictor oscillate when a program alternates between two access shapes, and the standard fix is to store more patterns, which costs area. A probabilistic update keeps one pattern per entry and lets it drift toward the union or the intersection depending on how often each bit actually appears, so the adaptivity comes out of the update rule rather than out of storage.
items.background_md: A hardware prefetcher watches the addresses a core requests and issues reads nobody asked for, so the line is already in cache when the instruction that needs it arrives. It is judged on three quantities that trade against one another: coverage, the share of misses it removes; accuracy, the share of its guesses that are ever used; and traffic, the extra bytes it drags off DRAM. Traffic is the one that bites on a multicore part, because every useless prefetch spends bandwidth some other core wanted, so an aggressive prefetcher can make a loaded machine slower.
items.deeper_md:
Proba fits in 10.04 KiB of storage — a 360 B first-offset table, a 1024 B active generation table, a 1024 B Bloom-style jail table that only records whether a region is still live, and three 2624 B pattern history tables indexed by PC-only, PC+offset and offset+offset. That is less than SMS at 11.95 KiB and Bingo at 13.20 KiB. Each entry carries a three-bit state selecting a (p, q) pair, moved toward coverage or toward accuracy by a local accuracy metric against an 80% threshold. In trace-based ChampSim at L2, the SPECspeed 2017 geometric mean is 6.6% speedup for 8.5% extra DRAM traffic, against PMP's 5.6% for 28.1% and Gaze's 5.0% for 12.4%; prefetch accuracy is 80.7% against SMS 77.0%, PMP 66.3% and Gaze 62.9%. Four-core CloudSuite gains 7.9%.

Two things to hold against it. LLC coverage is 50.9%, below PMP's 57.5% — deliberate, since low-value prefetches are suppressed, but it is a real loss on workloads where bandwidth is free. And the intermediate (p, q) states were tuned on SPECspeed 2017, which is also the headline evaluation suite. No independent replication exists; the artifact is the only check, and it wants about three hours per configuration on a 40-core machine.

glossary.definition: The first access into a fixed-size memory region, which starts a generation and is the event the predictor is indexed on; the bet is that the same code touching a new region will touch the same offsets within it.
The table holding one learned bit-vector per trigger, saying which lines of a region were used; a hit on a trigger replays that vector as prefetches, so the table's update policy is the whole design.
A compact dual-bitmap structure that records only whether a region's generation is still open, without storing its pattern, so more generations can be tracked for the same storage.

The trace-driven simulator the prefetching community competes in, maintained at Texas A&M; it replays recorded instruction traces, so it models timing but not the operating system or the real memory controller.

items.title: Separate the two searches and 187 kernel data races fall out
items.dek: Cen Zhang, Jia-Ju Bai and two co-authors stopped exploring thread interleavings while fuzzing the Linux kernel, queued only the inputs that had already shown two conflicting memory accesses land close together in time, and spent the expensive scheduling on those alone.
items.why_it_matters: Hunting a kernel data race means searching two spaces at once, and forcing a particular interleaving costs far more than generating another input, because the scheduler has to replay enough syscall history to rebuild kernel state before it can delay the access it cares about. Spending that budget only on inputs with a measured near-miss is what moves the yield: 79 confirmed races in a day against 19 for SegFuzz and 11 for CONZZER on the same hardware.
items.background_md: A data race is two threads touching one location with at least one write and no ordering between them. Compilers and processors are permitted to assume races do not occur, so a racy plain read can be split, reordered, or replaced by a value cached from earlier, and the resulting bug shows up only under one timing. The kernel's own detector, KCSAN, samples: it plants a software watchpoint on an access, stalls that thread for a randomised delay, and reports a race if a conflicting access arrives inside the window. Anything it does not sample, it does not see.
items.deeper_md:
The unit of evidence is a May Race Pair — conflicting accesses from different threads observed within a time threshold τ. Stage one runs syzkaller-style fuzzing of two-syscall groups with no scheduling control at all, keeping inputs that produce new MRPs and using an LLM to mutate the groups semantically. A backpressure controller moves τ itself: tighter when the scheduling queue backs up, looser when the scheduler starves. Stage two replays a bounded syscall history to recover kernel state, matches which occurrence of the access to delay, and backs off candidates that keep failing.

Over three weeks across eight modules — XFS, Btrfs, PTMX, OSS DSP, Bluetooth, F2FS, JFS and Floppy — on Linux 6.17 it found 187 unique races, 59 judged harmful; all 59 were reported, 39 confirmed by maintainers and 15 fixed by submission. Ablations put dynamic τ at 76 confirmed races against 55 for the best fixed τ, and full scheduling at 83 against 35 with history recovery removed.

The honest caveats: an MRP is a scheduling hint, not a race, and address reuse manufactures spurious pairs; the 187 figure is a multi-week campaign while every comparison number is a 24-hour run; and the mutation step depends on a remote model, 14.01 million tokens across eight runs.

glossary.definition: Two conflicting accesses from different threads seen within τ of each other during uncontrolled execution; it proves the accesses can come close in time, which is the precondition for a race but not the race itself.
The time window inside which two conflicting accesses count as a near-miss; too tight and almost nothing qualifies, too loose and the queue fills with pairs that will never actually interleave.

The kernel's compile-time-instrumented race detector, which samples accesses and deliberately stalls one thread to widen the race window; it accepts missed races in exchange for almost no false reports.
The split used here between races whose outcome can corrupt state or crash the kernel and races on values where any interleaving is acceptable; only 59 of the 187 were in the first class.

sources.title: Breaking the Coupling: Efficient Concurrency Fuzzing for Linux Kernel Data Race Detection

items.title: When a collision is guaranteed, finding it is now subexponential
items.dek: Deepak Bhati, Pranjal Dutta, Antoine Joux, Mahesh Sreekumar Rajasree and Karol Wegrzycki gave a deterministic algorithm that finds two subsets of n integers with equal sums in poly(n)·M^o(1) time whenever the largest integer M stays below 2^n.
items.why_it_matters: Equal Subset Sum is NP-complete in general, but once M is small enough the pigeonhole principle guarantees a colliding pair exists, so the question stops being whether one exists and becomes what it costs to exhibit one. That is a different problem with a different answer, and the paper pins it from both sides: the algorithm beats the previous poly(n)·M^(1/3) once the instance is dense enough, and a conditional lower bound says the exponent cannot move much further without a genuine advance on lattice problems.
items.background_md: Given n positive integers, Equal Subset Sum asks for two different subsets with the same total. There are 2^n subsets and every sum lies between 0 and n·M, where M is the largest integer, so once 2^n exceeds that range two subsets must collide. Existence then costs nothing to establish; all the work is in producing a witness. That shape recurs across computer science — an object is known to exist by a counting argument, and the only open question is the price of construction — and it is where the gap between a proof and an algorithm is widest.
items.deeper_md:
The algorithm runs in poly(n)·M^O(1/log δ), where δ = n/log M is the instance density; for M = 2^o(n) that is poly(n)·M^o(1), and it beats the previous poly(n)·M^(1/3) of Jin, Williams and Zhang once δ exceeds 19. The mechanism is pruned merging: split the input into k blocks, enumerate each block's subset sums, then merge the lists pairwise while keeping, at level j, only sums congruent modulo W^j with W about 2^(n/2k) — Karmarkar–Karp differencing used as a filter. When the final modulus exceeds the largest possible sum, a surviving congruent pair is an equal pair.

The lower bound is the part worth arguing with, because it is conditional on a hypothesis the authors admit is new in this form: a worst-case fine-grained assumption about the nth successive minima problem on lattices, which they say is stronger than the assumption of Vafa and Vaikuntanathan. Under it, nothing runs in 2^o(n/log n), even at density n^(1/2+o(1)). The reduction samples lattice points, writes them as integers in a large base, and decodes a collision into a short nonzero lattice vector. Average case, with M = Θ(2^n) and uniform integers, it finds a collision in Õ(2^(n/4)) with probability Ω(n^−2).

glossary.definition: The ratio n/log M of how many integers you have to how many bits each one carries; high density means many more subsets than available sums, so collisions are abundant and easier to stumble into.
A running time whose exponent on M shrinks toward zero as the instance grows, so the cost is eventually below M raised to any fixed positive power — subexponential in n without being polynomial.

Finding n short, linearly independent vectors in a lattice; its assumed worst-case hardness is the floor underneath much of post-quantum cryptography, which is why a reduction to it is a strong statement.

A heuristic for splitting numbers into balanced groups by repeatedly replacing the two largest with their difference; here the same idea is used to discard partial sums that cannot lead to a collision.

items.title: A looped model can share one KV cache, if it was trained to
items.dek: Hayden Prairie, Jacob Ryan, Taylor Berg-Kirkpatrick and Daniel Fu showed that a language model which runs the same block of layers several times can reuse the final pass's key-value cache for all the earlier passes — but only if its pretraining sampled the number of passes at random.
items.why_it_matters: A looped model holds its parameter count fixed while adding effective depth, which is the entire reason to build one, yet its inference memory still grows linearly with the number of passes because every pass caches its own keys and values. Sharing one cache breaks that coupling, and it breaks it where serving is actually constrained: a 1.3-billion-parameter model at batch 64 and 2,048 tokens of context drops from 63.82 GB of high-bandwidth memory to 21.60 GB.
items.background_md: A transformer keeps, for every token it has already read, the key and value vectors each attention layer computed — the KV cache — so generating the next token does not mean re-reading the whole context. That cache is the part of serving which scales with context length and batch size, and on an accelerator it competes with the weights for the same high-bandwidth memory. A looped or recurrent-depth model runs one block of layers repeatedly rather than stacking distinct ones, holding parameters constant while deepening the computation; each repetition is a fresh pass through attention, so each repetition builds its own cache.
items.deeper_md:
Shareability is not a property models simply have. Among the Parcae-style checkpoints pretrained on over 100 billion tokens, the 140M and 370M models tolerate sharing and the 770M, 1.3B and the ACT-trained Ouro models do not. The fix has two parts. During pretraining, the recurrence count per sequence is drawn from a Poisson with mean μ_rec and backpropagation is truncated to ⌊μ_rec/2⌋ passes, which the authors argue makes the residual dynamics contractive so successive caches converge toward a common limit. After pretraining, BeNice! adds γ·CE(y, p^(1←T)) to the loss, scoring the first recurrence when it is run against the final recurrence's keys and values. The failure they diagnose is specific: a token-independent residual error in the first layer of the first recurrence, a basis shift rather than noise. At 770M, shared validation perplexity goes from 21.61 under ordinary finetuning to 11.86, which is the unshared number.

The serving figures are simulated, not deployed: Mooncake traces replayed against proxy models built by looping GLM 4.7-FP8 blocks, giving up to 31.4% better cache hit rate and p90 time-to-first-token falling from 139.2 s to 23.2 s. Quality results are on Parcae only.

glossary.definition: How many times the shared block is run for one forward pass; raising it buys depth at no parameter cost and, without cache sharing, costs one more KV cache per step.
Training with the number of layers or passes drawn at random per example, so the network cannot rely on a fixed depth; here it is what pushes each pass's keys and values toward the same values.
The exponential of a model's average per-token loss, so roughly how many equally likely words it is choosing among; 21.61 versus 11.86 is a model that has lost the thread versus one that has not.
The latency before the first output token that nine requests in ten beat; it is dominated by whether the prompt's cache is already resident, which is why cache size shows up as a latency number.

foundations.subtitle: 36,864 words of program woven into wire by hand, and a scheduler that saved a landing by throwing work away.
foundations.tldr: The computer that flew Apollo had 2,048 words it could write to and 36,864 words it could only read, and the read-only part was literally woven: a wire threaded through a magnetic ring was a one, a wire passed around that same ring was a zero. That one manufacturing fact shaped everything above it — a program frozen months before launch, an interpreter that traded speed for code size, and a scheduler with eight job slots. When the slots ran out during the first lunar descent, the computer restarted and discarded whatever had not been marked essential, which is the only reason the landing continued.

sections.heading: A memory you cannot change, because it is woven
sections.body_md:
Start from the constraint. In the mid-1960s, writable memory meant ferrite cores, one core per bit, with three wires through each. That is expensive in volume and in wiring, and a program held that way can be corrupted by a power transient. What Apollo needed was tens of thousands of words that could not be disturbed by anything — and could be packed into roughly a cubic foot along with the rest of the machine.

Core rope answers both. Each module holds 512 cores, permalloy ribbon wound on a bobbin, about 0.249 inches across — large, deliberately. Through each core run 192 sense wires, twelve groups of sixteen, one group per stored word. A wire that passes through the core is a one. A wire routed around the outside of that same core is a zero. Flip the core's magnetisation with a current pulse and every wire threaded through it picks up an induced voltage; the wires that went around it pick up nothing. The data is the geometry.
sections.deeper_md: The density argument is the whole reason it was worth the trouble: about 1,500 bits per cubic inch including drivers and packaging, roughly five times what erasable core achieved, because one core carries 192 bits instead of one. 512 cores × 12 words gives 6,144 words per module, and six modules give the 36,864-word fixed store. One detail that follows from the parity scheme: words carry odd parity, so at most 15 of the 16 bits in a word are ever high, which caps the sense wires actually threaded through a core at 180 rather than 192. Block I modules were wired differently — 128 sense wires per core, eight words, 4,096 words per module.

sections.heading: Addressing by suppression, not by selection
sections.body_md:
Here is the part that reads backwards the first time. You do not select a core and pulse it. The set current runs through every core in a plane at once, which on its own would flip all of them. What picks out one core is a set of inhibit lines carrying opposing current, driven from the address bits, arranged so that every core except the wanted one has at least one active inhibit cancelling the set. The selected core is the one nothing is stopping.

Seven address bits choose one of 128 cores within a plane. Four reset lines select which of the four planes is live, and two set lines cover the planes in pairs. An additional pair of inhibit lines encodes address parity, which guarantees that every unselected core receives at least two inhibit signals rather than relying on one. A resistor-and-diode network ahead of all this picks the module and the strand.

The selection logic is therefore mostly a large network of current sources doing cancellation arithmetic, and that is why it dominates the module's volume and power rather than the cores themselves.
sections.deeper_md: There is a subtlety in the instruction timing that shows the hardware and the instruction decoder were designed together. A fixed-memory read begins before the decoder has finished establishing whether the operation applies to that address, so there is a clear line whose only job is to reset a core whose read had already started and turned out to be unwanted. Speculation plus a squash signal, in 1965, in current-steering hardware.

sections.heading: Eight weeks of weaving is a schedule constraint
sections.body_md:
Raytheon built the ropes in Waltham, Massachusetts, and a module took about eight weeks to wire. That is the number with consequences. Software had to be frozen months before a launch, because there was no patch mechanism short of weaving a new module and qualifying it; management treated the weaving lead time as a control on late changes, which it was.

The workforce came from the surrounding industry — women hired out of local textile mills and the Waltham Watch Company for their hands. The common wiring, the set, reset and inhibit lines that run through every core, was done by two people passing a hollow needle carrying wire back and forth. The sense wiring, where the data lives, was later semi-automated: the YUL assembler emitted a Mylar punched tape, the tape drove a machine that positioned the correct core under an aperture, and a worker threaded the sense wire through it, after which a nylon pin held it in place and an automated tester checked the result.

Each flight had a person responsible for its rope, the rope mother. For LUMINARY, the lunar module program, that was Margaret Hamilton.
sections.deeper_md: Each module cost roughly $15,000 to wire, which is a modest figure beside the program but a large one per bit, and it explains why the ropes end with a checksum word — a bugger word — chosen so each bank's checksum comes to a known value. A mis-threaded sense wire is a permanent, unfixable bit error in a part that took two months to make, so the verification had to be arithmetic rather than visual.

sections.heading: Fifteen bits, two NOR gates per latch, 11.7 microseconds
sections.body_md:
The processor is built out of one part: a dual three-input NOR gate, six transistors and eight resistors on a die, in a Fairchild resistor-transistor-logic flat pack. Block II used about 2,800 of them. A four-bit slice of the arithmetic unit is two boards of 60 chips, so 240 NOR gates per slice, and every register bit is a set-reset latch made of two cross-coupled NOR gates with gates to read it onto and write it off the bus.

A word is 16 bits: 15 of data and one of parity, with the data in ones' complement so that negating a number is bit inversion and there are two representations of zero. Instructions are a three-bit opcode and a twelve-bit address.

Timing is built from twelve time steps of just under a microsecond, making a memory cycle time of 11.7 microseconds. A typical instruction takes two of those — 23.4 microseconds, about 43,000 instructions per second. A 15-bit add is one instruction time; a multiply is two, 46.8 microseconds. The whole computer is 70 pounds, under a cubic foot, and 70 watts off a 28-volt supply.
sections.deeper_md: The uniformity is the design decision worth noticing. Using one logic part everywhere costs transistor efficiency — NOR-only logic needs more gates than a mixed family — and buys qualification: one part to screen, one failure mode to characterise, one supplier to audit. That trade, reliability bought with gate count, is the opposite of the trade a commercial machine of the same year would have made, and it is why the AGC was among the first computers to use integrated circuits in volume at all.

sections.heading: A scheduler with eight slots
sections.body_md:
Above the hardware sits the Executive, and it is a priority scheduler of a kind that would be recognisable in any real-time operating system today. Work comes in two flavours. A job has a priority, runs until something higher priority appears, and needs somewhere to keep its registers while it is suspended — a core set, twelve registers of erasable memory. A job doing vector or matrix arithmetic through the interpreter needs more scratch space on top, a VAC area of 43 registers. Short, strictly time-triggered work is not a job at all; it goes on WAITLIST, runs off its own interrupt, and must finish quickly, often by queueing a job to deal with whatever it found.

The resource limits are small and hard. There are eight core sets and five VAC areas. So at most eight jobs can be outstanding and at most five of those can be interpretive. There is no allocation failure mode that degrades gracefully: if a job asks for a core set and none is free, the Executive has nothing to give it.

That is the shape of the whole design. Fixed, countable resources, known at assembly time, with no dynamic allocation anywhere.
sections.deeper_md: You can read the arithmetic straight out of the Luminary 099 listing. EXECUTIVE.agc declares `NO.CORES DEC 7` with `COREINC` annotated "12 REGISTERS PER CORE SET", and a nearby comment reads "SEVEN SETS OF ELEVEN REGISTERS EACH" — the comments contradict each other and both contradict Don Eyles, who wrote much of this code and gives eight sets of twelve. The constant is a zero-based bound, so eight is right. It is a good reminder that a listing's comments are not a specification.

sections.heading: 1202, and why discarding work was the correct answer
sections.body_md:
On Apollo 11's descent the rendezvous radar was left in a mode where its antenna angle resolvers kept driving the guidance computer's counter interfaces. The radar's 800 Hz reference supply was not phase-locked to the computer's, and when the phase difference sat near 90 or 270 degrees the counters were stepped at up to 6,400 pulses per second per angle. Each counter increment steals one 11.7 microsecond memory cycle. That is about 13 percent of the machine's time — Grumman's later testing put the worst case at 13.36 percent — against a margin of 10 percent or less once the crew had a landing-data display running.

So SERVICER, the main guidance job that must complete within its two-second cycle, did not. It left core sets and VAC areas unreleased, the Executive ran out of both, and it raised the two alarms the astronauts read out: 1202 for no core set available, 1201 for no VAC area.

Both alarms call BAILOUT, which restarts the software. The restart is the feature, not the failure. It threw away the stale accumulating work and the unprotected display monitor, which freed exactly the resources that had run out.
sections.deeper_md: Restart protection is what makes a restart safe, and it is a discipline in the source rather than a mechanism in the hardware. Code that updates state computes the new value into a temporary, registers a waypoint, then commits — so if a restart jumps back to the last waypoint the update is not applied twice. After a restart each job resumes from its waypoint, only the most recent copy of a queued job is restarted, and any computation not marked protected is simply dropped. The visible evidence on Apollo 11 is that the display reverted from Noun 68 to Noun 63: the Noun 68 monitor was not restart-protected, so it was one of the things discarded. Restarts can also be raised by hardware — a power transient, the watchdog catching an endless loop, or a parity failure reading fixed memory.

glossary.definition: Read-only memory in which each ferrite core is shared by many words and the data is set by whether a given sense wire was threaded through that core or routed around it; 192 wires per core here, so one core holds twelve 16-bit words.
A wire carrying current opposed to the set current, used to stop a core flipping; because every unselected core gets at least one, addressing works by cancelling everywhere except the target.
Twelve words of erasable memory reserved to hold one suspended job's registers; there are eight, so eight is the hard ceiling on outstanding jobs and running out of them is alarm 1202.
Forty-three further words of scratch space needed by any job that uses the interpreter's vector and matrix operations; there are five, and exhausting them is alarm 1201.
11.7 microseconds, the time to read or write one word, and the unit the whole machine is priced in — an instruction is two of them and an unwanted counter increment is one.

A convention in which code marks a waypoint before committing a state change, so that software which resumes from that waypoint after a restart does not apply the change twice; unmarked work is discarded instead.

A signed number representation in which negation is bitwise inversion, which makes the adder simpler and gives two encodings of zero — the AGC uses the negative one as a marker, for instance for an available core set.

foundations.try_this: Open EXECUTIVE.agc in the Virtual AGC listing of Luminary 099, the Apollo 11 lunar-module program, and find the three statements that disagree: `NO.CORES DEC 7`, the `COREINC` comment reading "12 REGISTERS PER CORE SET", and the comment reading "SEVEN SETS OF ELEVEN REGISTERS EACH". Then find the `OCT 1201` and `OCT 1202` constants next to their `TC BAILOUT1` calls and read the one-line comments beside them. Finish with the alarm section of Don Eyles's own account; he wrote this code, and reading his explanation against the listing is the fastest way to see what a bounded-resource scheduler actually looks like when it fails.
